newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - BoF's Trichet says solid euro needed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BoF's Trichet says solid euro needed.

text.p: Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet called on Tuesday for a solid common European currency, saying it was essential to preserve low interest rates and solid economic growth in Europe.

"The euro has to be as solid, credible and confidence-inspiring as the franc today or naturally the Deutschemark today or the guilder today," Trichet said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"Because to create the best basis for solid growth -- for stable, strong growth -- you need low market interest rates and you will not get low market interest rates if you have a euro which is not solid and credible."

In the interview, conducted after Trichet had presented the Bank's annual report, he several times passed over opportunities to repeat previous robust calls for strict adherence to financial criteria in the Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).

"You have a treaty and the treaty says what it says," Trichet said when asked if he favoured a strict application of the treaty criteria. "You have to take into account that the French government has said we will implement EMU, we will make EMU on time on January 1, 1999."
"I am confident that the appropriate measures will be taken to reach that goal," he added.
Trichet's usual stance, repeated as recently as four months ago, is that only countries meeting Maastricht criteria could join EMU from the start.
"We hope the European members of the first (wave)...will be as numerous as possible on condition they respect the criteria in the treaty," he said in a radio interview on February 14.

Economists said the statement on Tuesday might be a sign that Trichet recognised that the euro would probably go forward even if countries did not rigidly respect the requirement that budget deficits represent no more than three percent of gross domestic product.

They said Trichet's call to apply the treaty was meant to satisfy international audiences, while demands for deficit cutting were aimed at France's new Socialist-led government, which has promised not to impose another round of austerity to meet Maastricht treaty goals.
"It's a mixture of external positioning with regard to Germany, while internally he still wants to pressure the government to cut deficits," said ABN Amro head of research Philippe Brossard.

Recent forecasts, among them a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, have shown that France and Germany will probably not meet the three percent deficit limit this year, the crucial target for qualification for the euro. The OECD said both France and Germany would post deficits of 3.2 percent of GDP.
French newspaper reports have suggested France's deficit to GDP ratio will be between 3.3 and 3.8 percent this year without new spending cuts.

Presenting the Bank's annual report, Trichet repeated his warning that France had to cut public spending and deficits and enact deep structural reforms to protect hard-won franc stability and preserve low market interest rates.
"Controlling public spending and reducing public deficits is indispensible in 1997 as it is in the medium term," he said.
